messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In these few lines, Majeed does **not** appear as the usual cunning and apathetic figure. He wakes someone, states a plan, and physically carries Jamila while Rahima follows. The immediate effect is urgency and protection, not indifference. The only “cunning” is possible in his strategy: he chooses the village, uses the night, and controls the movement. Apathy, however, is absent.

As for motive, the passage is ambiguous. If he acts because it is his duty to protect the vulnerable, the scene has a **deontological** or good-will shape. But the action is also strongly goal-directed: the end is safety, the village, escape. Given Majeed’s established cunning, it is fair to say his act is at least partly **teleological**—saving them as a calculated means, even if it may also contain genuine concern. I would not call it pure deontology; I would call it protective behavior with likely calculated purpose.

Palindrome words included: racecar, rotor, kayak, radar, madam, level, civic, stats, rotator, deified.
